A GLASS OF MILK

In a small town, there lived a poor little boy who used to do odd jobs
like selling different objects from door to door. The money he earned from
those jobs was used to buy his daily food and pay his school expenses. It was
a usual day of selling items from house to house when he felt very hungry and
sick. He was so famished that he couldn’t even walk any more steps. With
enough strength, he decided to ask for food at a house in the neighborhood.
When the poor boy knocked on the door of a house, a beautiful young girl
opened the door to his surprise. With much hesitation, he requested the
young girl for a glass of water. The boy said, “Can you please give me a glass
of water?” The pretty girl was taken aback after seeing the poor boy’s condition
and understood how hungry he was. She said, “Sure, wait a minute.” She
went into the kitchen, and instead of a glass of water as requested by the little
boy, she brought him a glass of milk. “Here, little boy. Drink it!” said the young
girl. The boy was astonished to see the glass of milk in front of him. He drank
the milk and felt better than ever. After drinking the milk, the boy thanked
the kind-hearted girl and asked her, “How much do I owe you for this milk?”
“Oh dear, I don’t want any money for this”, the girl replied softly. The
boy thanked the compassionate girl from the bottom of his heart and then left
the place. Years passed by. The young girl grew up into a beautiful grown
woman. One day she fell severely ill and was taken to the hospital. There, she
had some tests, which unfortunately revealed that she had a rare neurological
disorder that required several treatments and great care for many months.
She was hospitalized at one of the city’s best hospitals as her health
deteriorated day by day. Dr Kevin, a well-known neuro specialist, was
assigned the girl’s case by the hospital. Dr Kevin found the girl’s illness hard
to cure despite his extraordinary expertise. However, he did not give up. The
treatment took months. With determination and much perseverance, Dr Kevin
successfully brought the girl’s ailment under control. The girl was finally
cured of the disease after careful observation and medication. Everyone in the
hospital complimented the doctor for his successful work. But the girl had
her own worries about the hospital bills. She thought to herself, “How will I
pay for such an extensive treatment when I have only a little money of my
own?” The girl’s family did not leave her enough money that could possibly
clear her extensive treatment and therapy in that reputed hospital. Finally,
the bill arrived. With shaking hands, she opened it and was astonished to see
that the bill had been cancelled across. Beneath the amount, there was a note
signed by her treatment doctor, Dr Kevin. The note said, “Bill paid in full years
ago with a glass of milk!” The girl remembered the young boy she had helped
years ago and felt happy.

A LOST CIVILIZATION

A long, long time ago, thousands of years before there were cities in any
place in the world, wandering hunters from the Asia mainland crossed the
narrow channel to Alaska.
These people who were called Indians slowly spread over the two American
continents. Some of them remained hunters, the others became farmers and
built great cities. From these Indians descended a distinctive group called the
Mayas.

The Mayas had cities long before any white man landed in the American
continent. By the seventh century A.D. they had built many cities in Central
America. The ruins of these cities could still be found standing in the jungles
of Central America. The most famous of these cities was called "Chichen Itza".
In its ruins were found many beautiful buildings, terraces, temples, and a
great plaza with many courts. The palaces and monasteries were built for their
nobles and priests. There was even an observatory for studying the stars and
their movements and other meteorological researches:

The priests carefully watched the movements of the stars. They made a
calendar which was as accurate as the one we use today. It was more accurate
than the calendars used in Europe and Asia at that time.

The Mayas dressed in the fine locks. They wore gold ornaments. Most
precious among their ornaments were of jade. Jades and rich plume feathers
were worn only by the rich and the powerful nobles and priests.
They used a system of writing similar to the ancient Babylonians using
character symbols because they had no alphabet. They wrote books on their
history, astronomy, and religion. Many of these books, however, have been
lost. Only three are in existence today.

The Mayan engineers made fine roads similar to those built by the
Romans at the height of their power. They used layers of limestone fill the
roadway and gravel to fill in the crevices. They then covered the surface with
fine limestone which acted as a sort of cement. A heavy road-roller hewn by
hand out of hard stone was rolled over the road over and over again. The
rollers were so heavy. It took 15 to 20 men to work them over the roads. The
roads they made were very good. With little repairs, they have been used until
recent times.
The farmers among the Mayas lived in villages outside the cities. They
raised crops and built roads, temples and palaces, had no wheeled vehicle nor
tamed beasts of burden. They used their own muscles to carry heavy loads.
How amazing therefore that they did build magnificent roads and
temples and palaces with their own puny hands!

I REFUSE

The life story of Dr. Jose Rizal has been told and retold many, many
times that almost all the intimate details of his life are well known to us. But
very little has been written of Jose Rizal's mother, Doña Teodora Alonzo. Do
many of us know, for example, that she refused to accept pension offered to
her by the Philippine government?

Doña Teodora, the mother who gave our nation the neatest Malayan,
is a heroine in her own right. She had suffered imprisonment for just being
Jose Rizal's mother. She suffered more than any other mother in Philippine
history for raising and educating her son. Jose.

The Rizal family had been impoverished because of Dr. Rizal's
struggles against Spanish tyranny. Doña Teodora found herself in
straightened circumstances years after the death of our hero. Therefore, she
rightfully deserved the pension offered her by our government.

In 1908, the Philippine Legislature, aware of Doña Teodora's need,
unanimously agreed to grant her a life pension as a token of the gratitude of
the Filipino people. At that time, she was residing in the house of one of her
daughters in Manila. A delegation of lawmakers was appointed to advise her
of the pension. The delegation thanked her for the patriotic service to her
country and people and told her that the government was giving her a
substantial pension which would make her comfortable and secure during
her remaining years.

"A substantial pension is offered to you as a token of the nation's
gratitude for your patriotism, Doña Teodora, "the chairman of the delegation
said.

Doña Teodora firmly but politely refused to accept the pension. "Our
family is not patriotic because of mercenary motives," she told the group of
delegation. "If the government has enough money to offer me a life pension, it
should give this money to the poor who deserve it more. I have my children
and relatives to take care of me," Doña Teodora continued.

Thus, the mother of our greatest hero proved herself worthy as a
mother of a heroic son. What a contrast to our present-day so-called "heroes"
and "patriots" who not only clamor for pensions and backpays but also, to
add insult to injury, claim that they deserve them. Hear howl when action on
their application is delayed. They could not wait until their services were given
just rewards and recognition.

Doña Teodora's self- abnegation should serve as a lesson to our
pension-·hungry and so- called "heroes" and patriots who mask their greed in
the guise of patriotism.

THE ENCHANTED TRUNK

There once lived a fairy in a big balete tree near the mouth of a cave.
She was known as Macaban. Unlike other fairies, she was visible most of the
time. She had brown eyes and curly hair. Her voice was sweet and was always
kind. She was very generous. She was always ready to help the unfortunate,
and she comforted them in their sorrows. She gave food and clothing to the poor.
During wedding, she would lend the bridegroom his wedding attire, precious
stones, gold tablewares, kitchen utensils, which she kept in storerooms inside
an underground city. Anybody could utter his request at the keyhole; the
stone door would open at once to let him in and select the things he needed.

The goodness of Macaban was everywhere. The borrowers came not
only from Inabangan but also from neighboring towns.

One day, a dishonest couple came to borrow some wedding attire,
jewels and tableware for their son's wedding. They were allowed to enter the
city storerooms to get the things they needed. Seeing that nobody kept watch,
they picked up several precious objects and put them in their bags and
pockets. When they went out of the door, they promised the door keeper to
return everything after the wedding, but they did not tell him of the jewels
that bulged in their pockets thinking that Macaban would never know.

After the wedding, the dishonest couple did not return the things they
borrowed. Instead, they went around the town and urged the people to destroy
the home of Macaban and to drive the fairy away.

Macaban was angry at what the dishonest couple did to her. So, she
thought of teaching them a lesson. She called all the people to enter the city
and select a gift for themselves. She gave them 20 minutes to select that they
liked best on condition that they must not stay more than the given time.

The honest people obeyed the command of Macaban for they stayed in
the storeroom for only the time allowed. On the other hand, the dishonest
couple went into the heart of the city collecting jewels and precious stones.
When the 20minutes were over, Macaban waved her hand. Deep water rushed
down the street separating the two high cliffs.

"Because you are dishonest, you must remain here forever," Macaban
cried, "You cannot cross the deep water and escape from the many crocodiles."

Until today, the keyhole, the mouth of the cave, and the stone door
can be seen by boat riders going up and down the Inabangan River in Bohol.
People say these parts of the enhanced trunk of Macaban, a splendid city
underneath the mountain.

Atalanta, a beautiful and fearless maiden, was the daughter of
Scheneus, King of Boetia. What she was most famous for was the fact that
she had the fastest pair of feet in the whole world.

Because of her beauty she had many suitors, but proud Atalanta would
not look with favor on any of them.

She said, "I will marry only the man who is a faster runner than l."

She told her suitors that whoever really wished to marry her would have
to run a race against her. If they failed, they would be put to death. Strangely
enough, many of her suitors tried. They lost the race and thus lost their lives.

Hippomenes, one of her suitors, watched every race and saw that he
could never win against Atalanta. Only a miracle would help him, so he went
to Venus, goddess of love and lovers for help.

Venus took pity on him and gave him three golden apples from her
garden in the island of Cyprus. She whispered to him the secret of how to use
the apples.

Happily, Hippomenes sought Atalanta and asked her permission to run
a race with him. Atalanta looked at the young man and her heart filled with
pity for him. She tried to persuade him not to try because he might lose his
life.

"I shall gladly die, for without you; life will not be worth living,
“Hippomenes said. Finally, with great reluctance, Atalanta agreed to run a
race with him.

"Venus, don't forsake me now," he whispered as they took their places
for the race.

Off they went. Hippomenes was fast but she gained on him and was
about to overtake him when he threw one of the golden apples on her path.
The girl was attracted by the glitter, so she paused one moment in her flight,
scooped up the apple from the ground and ran on.

covered the gap between them. Soon he heard the swift patter of her feet close
behind.

"Venus, kind goddess, do not abandon me now, "and he tossed the
second apple at the feet of Atlanta. For the second time, Atalanta paused,
scooped up the apple from the ground then ran on.

Hippomenes' lead did not do him much good for soon Atalanta was close
again at his heels and was about to pass him.

The goal was near His heart beating with joy, Hippomenes threw third
golden apple, and it rolled along Atalanta could not resist it. She paused only
a brief second and ran again. But before she could catch up with Hippomenes,

descendants.

North of the Philippines lies our closest neighbor. It is commonly known
as the Republic of China (R.O.C.), or in most international organizations, as

Taiwan was once a poor, underdeveloped country---enjoy a high

Bamboo huts have disappeared, replaced by brick stone houses.

Taiwan has succeeded because of its people. The average Taiwanese is
industrious and self-reliant and is a willing helper to his neighbor when
someone needs help.

magnificent homes as other underdeveloped countries do, Taiwan began with

providing security and livelihood for the tenants of big landholders. It opened

acres of Riceland. The former owners of large tracts of land were encouraged

immediate needs. They produce enough clothing materials. They have an

AFRICA, THE DARK CONTINENT
Whenever we think of Africa, we seem to picture a large continent
covered with either huge desert, high plateau and mountains, and vast
impenetrable jungles inhabited by black uncivilized people. We oftentimes
overlook the past that Egypt, which is part of Africa, was once cradle of the
first great civilization. Egypt had built magnificent temples, palaces, and the
pyramids when most on Europe was still in a barbaric stage.

Africa has often been called the Dark Continent. The true Africa is a
continent of vivid contrasts. There are many kinds of landforms and the
climate is variable. There are the hot desert Sahara Desert and the high
plateau which covers the area south of the Sahara. There are dense jungles,
broad fertile plains and high snow-capped mountains. As a result of these
differences, many ways of living have developed in Africa's varied kinds of
lands.

The areas north of the Sahara have been part of the rich and colorful
life of the Mediterranean world. Sahara's great expanse is not entirely a waste
of shifting sands. Only one-tenth of the desert is covered by sand. The rest
are plains, hills, mountains, and thousands of oases where date palms and
other palms thrive. Egypt and Ethiopia are regions which are productive,
culturally and agriculturally. Theirs is a rich history.
Both the eastern and western coastal areas are fertile. Here are cites of
the cities and other centers of population. Southern Africa is a pleasant land
and is one of the continent's most prosperous areas. Central Africa's rivers
have their source here.

Central Africa is covered with dense jungles. So much rain falls that
trees and plants grow very fast. Thick bushes and tough vines twinning from
trees make passage difficult, sometimes impossible. The jungles are inhabited
by pygmies who never mingle with other people.

They depend on fruits, roots, and small animals which they kill with
poisoned arrows. Elsewhere, the plateaus are grasslands with only a few trees.
The grasslands with all grass are the home of elephants, buffaloes, and
rhinoceros. The areas where the grass is not very tall are the roving areas of
all kinds of deer, giraffes, and zebras.

The African plateau is peopled by Negroes (Bantu)who have little
contact with civilization. They are very tall men; men seven feet in height are
common sight. Many of them earn their living through primitive farming,
hording, and hunting, they have a tribal form of government; each village has
a headman, usually related to the chief of the tribe. There are many war-like
tribes in the heart of Central Africa.

The civilized people of Africa are mostly Muslims. The Muslim Arabs
were the first people to have commercial and cultural contact with Africa.
Christian missionaries have made inroads in the establishment of
Christianity in many parts of Africa.

With these innovations, could we say then that Africa is no longer the
Dark Continent?

Select the letter of the correct answer.

by: Alberto G. Romulo

It is often said that it is difficult to make comparisons of two people,

for his political activities including speeches on political platforms and in the
Senate highly critical of the then Chief Executive.

THE SEA HORSE

Nature has many strange creatures, some of them huge, some of them
small. One of these strange creatures is the sea horse. This animal of the sea
has the arching neck of a wild stallion, the swelling bosom of a pigeon, the
grasping tail of a monkey, and the power to change its color that belongs to a
chameleon. It has eyes that pivot independently of one another so that while
one looks up, the other can look down or around. To top this fantasy, the
male-is equipped with a kangaroo style pouch in its front, from which the little
ones are born.

There are more than 40 species, ranging in length from one inch to one
foot, and they can be found in the warm seas all over the world. The sea is a
master of camouflaging. It can change color to go with its surroundings.

The sea horse's body is sheathed in a tough, Capiz-like armor of bony
plates. Because of this rigid armor, it swims standing up by fluttering a tiny
yellow, fanlike fin on its back, propelling itself in a stately manner. Straight
as a rod, it moves forward or backward, up and down, by manipulating that
fin so fast that movement is hardly visible. Two membrane- like fins at the
sides of its head wave carelessly.

The worst thing that can happen to a swimming sea horse is a puncture
in its armor. A single puncture in its armor could cause air to escape from its
sealed armor and make the sea horse sink helplessly to the bottom. There it
remains until he has manufactured enough gas to fill up his tank.

The courtship of sea horses is strange. The female produces from 500
to 600 eggs and deposits them in the male's pouch. For the next 45 days, the
father sea horse nourishes the nestling in his swelling incubator pouch. At
the end of this period, a baby sea horse the size of a comma swims out,
followed by another, then another. This continues until the whole brood is
ejected from the incubator. Each baby is an exact replica of its parents, except
that the body is transparent. Its tiny heart can be seen beating with aid of
magnifying glass.

The sea horse feeds on plankton and minute plant and animal life. It
would not feed on anything that is not alive and moving. The sea horse itself
is not fit to be eaten either by man or by fish.

What use is a sea horse? Studies made have not revealed any useful
purpose in the sea horse. However, everything in nature has a need and a
purpose. Perhaps, sea horses were made to keep the level of plankton down
so that the latter would not overrun the sea.

ABRAHAM LINCOLN

Many stories have been told of the boy who was born in a log cabin of
very poor parents; of how he learned to read by the light of the fireplace; and
of how he walked long distances to borrow books. From humble beginnings,
he rose and, became the Great Emancipator.

As a young man, he tended store for a neighbor. On one occasion he
unintentionally short-changed a customer. It was long after the customer had
departed when he discovered his mistake. He walked miles and miles to the
customer's house just to return the change. That was how he earned the name
"Honest Abe".

Then he became President of the United States. When he was troubled
by affairs of state, he took long walk to clear his mind. On these walks he was
usually dressed in his old clothes. With his long strides he often outdistanced
the men assigned to guard him.

At dusk of one winter, he went on one of these walks. Snow had covered
the roads making them slippery. He was walking along an almost deserted
street, when a carriage driving fast overtook him. Suddenly, a dog ran across
the street frightening the horses. They shied, driving the carriage to a deep
ditch, its rear wheel stuck in the deep muddy ditch. The horses were unable
to move the carriage no matter how they tired. The colored driver and the
footman kept urging the horses, but the carriage-wheel sank deeper.

The passenger, apparently a very wealthy and important man because
of his elegant and rich garb, keep shouting at his men, waving his arms in
anger and frustration. He had an appointment to keep at the White House.

The tall, bearded pedestrian came to the scene, and at a glance saw
what had happened. He approached the carriage on the side stuck in the
ditch, put his shoulders to the wheel, and signaled the coachman to prod the
horses. At first, the carriage would not move. With another mighty heave of
the tall pedestrian, the carriage finally moved out of the ditch. The coachman
leaped to his place, the passenger sank to his seat, and the carriage drove on
to the White House.

The passenger was just on tome for his appointment. In the President's
room, he sat, a little impatient. In his country, he was an important man. In
this wild. country, he did not relish being kept waiting.

At last, a door opened. A tall, bearded man entered, his clothes
splattered with mud and snow. He gravely took the suddenly limp hand of the
dumb- stricken visitor, then went around the desk and, mud and all, sat on
the chair of the President of the United States.

Etched on an old-fashioned ink stand on which the tall man dipped a
quill pen was the name: A. Lincoln!
